Incorporating this into an explicit hierarchical network (H-Net) allows replacing the (implicitly hierarchical) tokenization–LM–detokenization pipeline with a single model learned fully end-to-end [HNET Abstract].

text: Mimi encodes audio with a causal auto‑encoder that first projects a 24 kHz waveform into a latent space and then discretizes that latent using a Residual Vector Quantizer, which iteratively applies vector quantization to the residuals of each quantizer level [MOSHI §3.3.1].

During training, Mimi distills non‑causal, high‑level semantic information from a self‑supervised speech model (WavLM) into the tokens produced by its causal model, so the first level of acoustic tokens carries semantic content while later levels capture fine acoustic detail [MOSHI §3.3].
The residual‑vector‑quantization bottleneck therefore yields a hierarchy of tokens that jointly represent semantic and acoustic information [MOSHI §3.3.1].

Because all convolutions in Mimi’s encoder are causal, the encoder and decoder can operate in a streaming fashion, enabling real‑time encoding and decoding of the combined semantic‑acoustic token stream [MOSHI §3.3.1].

This causal design is essential for Moshi’s real‑time spoken‑dialogue system, allowing low‑latency generation (the system achieves a theoretical 160 ms latency) while maintaining the ability to predict tokens incrementally as audio arrives [MOSHI §7].

text: Inner Monologue is a training and inference setup for Moshi that decomposes speech into a hierarchical chain of text, semantic and acoustic tokens and predicts this structured sequence in a hierarchical manner, allowing the model to represent each utterance both as text and speech and to generate arbitrary voices [MOSHI §2].

It incorporates time‑aligned text tokens by inserting a text stream W, obtained from SentencePiece tokenisation of the audio transcription, as the first sub‑sequence in the joint token sequence V, so that the text tokens act as a prefix to the generation of semantic tokens [MOSHI §3.4.4].

This textual prefix provides a scaffolding that increases the linguistic quality of the generated speech, as shown by ablation studies where Inner Monologue had one of the most critical impacts on speech quality [MOSHI §3.4.4].

By introducing a configurable delay between the text sequence W_t and the audio tokens A_t,q, the model can control which modality dictates the content: placing audio ahead of text makes the text follow the sampled audio, yielding a streaming ASR model; placing text ahead of audio makes the audio follow the text, yielding a streaming TTS model [MOSHI §3.4.4].

text: The pipeline begins with raw byte‑level input that is first passed through a small encoder network, which transforms the bytes into initial vector representations and prepares them for compression [HNET §1].

Next, the dynamic chunking (DC) module receives these encoder outputs and, using a routing module that predicts boundary scores together with a smoothing module that interpolates uncertain boundaries, groups adjacent vectors into content‑aware chunks while optionally down‑sampling the sequence length [HNET §1].

The resulting compressed chunk representations are then fed to the main network, which contains the bulk of the model parameters and can be any standard token‑based architecture such as a Transformer or state‑space model, operating on the learned chunk tokens [HNET §1].

After the main network processes the chunks, a dechunking layer reconstructs the original resolution: a smoothing module converts the discrete chunk outputs into interpolated vectors and an upsampler restores them to the full sequence length using the boundary indicators produced by the router [HNET Figure 1].
Finally, the decoder network receives the upsampled vectors and maps them back to the raw byte space, completing the autoregressive generation of the next bytes [HNET §1].

The authors identify three major limitations of conventional spoken dialogue systems: first, the latency that accumulates across separate components, resulting in a typical global latency of several seconds, which is far from the few‑hundred‑millisecond response times of natural conversations [MOSHI §1]; second, the loss of non‑written information such as emotion, accent, and non‑speech audio because language understanding and generation occur in the textual domain, ignoring paralinguistic cues [MOSHI §1]; and third, the turn‑based modeling that assumes well‑defined single‑speaker segments, which fails to capture interruptions, overlapping speech—accounting for 10 to 20% of spoken time—and backchanneling [MOSHI §1].

Moshi’s speech‑to‑speech approach addresses these limitations by: (1) removing the need for separate speech recognition and text‑to‑speech modules, thereby reducing latency to a theoretical 160 ms and enabling real‑time interaction [MOSHI §7]; (2) generating speech directly from audio tokens, thus preserving non‑linguistic information and avoiding the textual bottleneck [MOSHI Abstract]; and (3) employing a multi‑stream architecture that processes input and output audio streams jointly, eliminating explicit speaker turns and allowing the model to handle overlapping speech, interruptions, and backchanneling in full‑duplex dialogue [MOSHI §3.1].

The papers state that conventional spoken‑dialogue pipelines suffer from (1) high latency caused by chaining many components, leading to “a typical global latency of several seconds” instead of the few hundred‑millisecond response times of natural conversation[MOSHI §1]; (2) loss of non‑linguistic information because language understanding and generation happen in the textual domain, so “any non‑written information is ignored by the model…paralinguistic information, such as emotion and accent, to non‑speech audio” is discarded[MOSHI §1]; and (3) a turn‑based architecture that assumes well‑defined single‑speaker segments, which “falls short in modeling aspects of spoken conversations such as interruptions, overlapping speech…and backchanneling”[MOSHI §1].

Moshi’s speech‑to‑speech design tackles these issues by (a) generating speech directly from a text‑LLM backbone using a neural audio codec, which eliminates the separate ASR and TTS stages and thus reduces latency to a theoretical 160 ms[MOSHI §1]; (b) modeling both text and audio tokens jointly (Inner Monologue) so that “the model … remains a speech‑to‑speech system” and can retain paralinguistic cues in the audio domain[MOSHI §3.1]; and (c) employing a multi‑stream Transformer architecture that “does not need to explicitly model speaker turns” and supports full‑duplex interaction, allowing overlapping speech and interruptions without a turn‑based constraint[MOSHI §3.1].
